title: iPhone X-Change
author: Darian Aghili (Fuqua '24)
prompt: Electronics Co. is a US distributor of secondhand phones, tablets, laptops, and other consumer electronics. It buys used devices from consumers and resells them through an online direct-to-consumer platform. Estimate the total US market size across used-device verticals to understand its opportunity.

clarifying_info.answer: Size the US secondhand-device market as soon as possible.

interviewer_notes: First ask the candidate to structure a top-down sizing method. Then provide volume sold, used share, US share, and ASP from Exhibit 1. The only available exhibit page also contains worked market sizes and the total answer, so its image must be hidden during practice even though the structured table contains inputs only.

suggested_framework.summary: Estimate annual units by vertical, narrow to used US transactions, multiply by secondhand ASP, and add adjacent electronics.

children.label: Population/eligible ages, ownership, replacement frequency, and device category
Used share, US share, channel penetration, and consumer willingness
Used ASP by phone, tablet, laptop, and other electronics
Growth, scalability, supply, quality, support, and customer retention

stages.interviewer_asks: How would you size the secondhand consumer-electronics market?
stages.expected_answer: For each vertical, estimate annual new-device transactions from eligible population, device ownership, and repurchase rate; multiply by the share bought used, the US share if starting globally, and used ASP. Sum phones, tablets, and laptops, then estimate adjacent products such as headphones, consoles, and cameras.
good_answer_signals: Includes replacement frequency and used share

stages.interviewer_asks: Calculate the TAM by vertical and in total.
stages.info_to_release: Phones: 1.25B volume, 20% used, 10% US, $50 ASP. Tablets: 160M, 15% used, 8.3% US, $150 ASP. Laptops: 220M, 5% used, 9.1% US, $200 ASP. Other electronics equal 20% of the combined phone, tablet, and laptop market.
stages.expected_answer: Phones: 1.25B x 20% x 10% x $50=$1.25B. Tablets: 160M x 15% x 8.3% x $150=$298.8M, about $300M. Laptops: 220M x 5% x 9.1% x $200=$200.2M, about $200M. Core total is $1.749B; other electronics add $349.8M. Exact TAM is $2.0988B, or $2.1B rounded.
good_answer_signals: Adds 20% only after summing the three

stages.interviewer_asks: What market insights should the CEO take away?
stages.expected_answer: The roughly $2.1B US market is sizeable and geographically scalable. Phones account for about 60% of TAM and are the clearest priority, with potential for deeper secondhand penetration. Reuse has an environmental value proposition, while tablets, laptops, and adjacent products provide diversification.

stages.interviewer_asks: Summarize the opportunity and principal risks.
stages.expected_answer: Electronics Co. addresses an approximately $2.1B US secondhand-electronics TAM, led by $1.25B phones, then about $300M tablets, $200M laptops, and $350M other devices. Prioritize phones while building quality-control and supply capabilities. Risks include demand for new models, scaling refurbishment quality, constrained device supply, weak customer stickiness, and legacy manufacturer support becoming obsolete.

exhibits.title: Market-size inputs
exhibits.description: Volume, used share, US share, and average secondhand price for phones, tablets, and laptops.
exhibits.key_insight: Phones dominate the used-device market; total TAM including other electronics is about $2.1B.

math.question: What is TAM by core device category?
What is total TAM including other electronics?

synthesis: The US secondhand-electronics TAM is approximately $2.1B: $1.25B phones, about $300M tablets, $200M laptops, and $350M other electronics. Focus first on phones while scaling supply and quality assurance, then expand adjacencies. Key risks are new-model preference, device supply, refurbishment quality, customer stickiness, and obsolete manufacturer support.
what_great_looks_like: Adds other products on the combined base
common_pitfalls: Applying percentages in the wrong order
Treating global volume as US volume
Adding 20% to each category and then again to total
Stopping at the number without implications

extraction.notes: Deduplication verdict was NEW. All TAM calculations were independently recomputed and match the source's rounded values.
